author.name: Arthur Conan Doyle
author.biography: Arthur Conan Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh and wrote the first Sherlock Holmes novel, A Study in Scarlet (1887), while practising as a doctor in Southsea. The twelve stories in this collection appeared month by month in The Strand Magazine from July 1891 to June 1892 and were published together as a book in 1892. Doyle also wrote historical novels, adventure stories and much else, but he kept returning to Holmes and Watson until the late 1920s.

hook.text: When does a trivial detail become the whole explanation?

paragraphs: A masked visitor wants a photograph recovered. A pawnbroker is paid to copy out an encyclopaedia by hand. A typist cannot find the man she was about to marry. Most of the stories begin with someone bringing a problem to Baker Street that sounds either absurd or trivial, and many turn on what Holmes notices while the visitor is still talking.

Watson tells the stories. By the opening case he is married, in medical practice and no longer sharing rooms with Holmes, so he arrives as a friend and witness. He admits when he is baffled, and the reader faces the same evidence he does before Holmes explains it.

Listen for the question that seems beside the point and for the details Watson mentions in passing: a sleeve, a boot, a newspaper advertisement, a sound in the night. Holmes is often right and sometimes theatrical about it. The endings vary, and not every truth he uncovers is handed to the police.
Each story is complete in itself and fills one chapter. Read them in order to watch the friendship and Holmes’s habits accumulate, or open any case on its own.

orientation.text: Twelve self-contained cases, one per chapter. Holmes and Watson appear throughout; nearly everyone else belongs to a single story.
